Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify the anatomic relationships of the shoulder.
Understand the anatomic forces that confer stability and mobility to the glenohumeral joint.
Understand the anatomy of the shoulder and the manner in which pathology contributes to
dysfunction.
Overview
The shoulder is a combination of articulations that allow for a large degree of motion and
function to place the arm in space.
The shoulder is composed of three diarthrodial joints (the glenohumeral, acromioclavicular,
and sternoclavicular joints) and the scapulothoracic articulation.


The combination of the shoulder’s limited bony constraint and complex soft-tissue structures
allows for a high degree of mobility while maintaining stability.

Overview
Despite the suggestion of its singular name, the shoulder is a combination of
articulations that allow for a large degree of motion and function to place the arm in
space. The shoulder is connected to the body by the sternoclavicular joint. The clavicle
acts as the mechanical strut to support the shoulder while the scapular body leverages
the motion of the shoulder against the posterior chest wall. The limited constraint of the
glenoid and proximal humerus is balanced by soft tissues and the dynamic forces of the
rotator cuff. A series of complex muscle attachments then act to facilitate shoulder
stabilization and motion. (Resource 1)
Osteology
Clavicle
The clavicle is the first bone to ossify (fifth week of gestation); it is the only long bone to ossify
via intramembranous ossification.
The medial (sternal) epiphysis is the last ossification center to fuse (age 20 to 25 years).
The clavicle is a flat S-shaped bone, with the medial aspect convex anterior and the lateral
segment convex posterior.
The primary blood supply is periosteal; no nutrient artery is present.

Clavicle
The clavicle, similar to other flat bones of the face and skull, forms via intramembranous
ossification. Dissimilar from the endochondral ossification process of long bones,
intramembranous ossification occurs via the aggregation of undifferentiated
mesenchymal cells, which then differentiate into osteoblasts. This process begins at
approximately the fifth week of gestation. At the time of birth, the clavicle is not fully
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
2/33

ossified, permitting the deformation of the shoulders during passage through the birth
canal. The medial epiphysis is the last ossification center to fuse, which occurs at
approximately age 20 to 25 years. The clavicle develops into an S-shaped morphology
(medial aspect convex anterior and the lateral segment convex posterior) with the distal
clavicle becoming noticeably flattened in shape. The blood supply to the clavicle is via its
periosteal supply, and no nutrient arteries are present.
Scapula
Ossification of the scapular body begins at the eighth week of gestation.
The acromion has three ossification centers: the meta-acromion (base), meso-acromion
(middle), and pre-acromion (tip). Failure of fusion results in os acromiale.
The scapular spine is an osseous ridge that separates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus
fossae.
The scapula has only one true diarthrodial articulation, the acromioclavicular joint.
The scapula typically spans the second to seventh ribs and has three borders (medial, lateral,
and inferior).
The scapular body is congruent to the contour of the curved chest wall. Therefore, the
scapular plane is 30° anterior relative to the true coronal plane of the body.
Normal shoulder motion is approximately two-thirds glenohumeral and one-third
scapulothoracic.
The relationship between acromial anatomy and rotator cuff disease remains controversial.
The classification of acromial morphology (flat, curved, or hooked) is challenged by poor
interobserver reliability.
The coracobrachialis muscle and the short head of the biceps tendon originate from the tip of
the coracoid process.
The pectoralis minor muscle inserts onto the medial coracoid process.
The suprascapular notch is located at the lateral portion of the superior scapular border,
medial to the base of the coracoid process. The suprascapular nerve traverses through the
notch below the transverse scapular ligament as the suprascapular artery courses above.
The spinoglenoid notch lies below the lateral border of the scapular spine. The suprascapular
artery and nerve pass through it before terminating at the infraspinatus fossae.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
3/33


Scapula
The scapular body begins ossification at the eighth week of gestation. Of clinical
importance, the acromion has three ossification centers, including the meta-acromion
(base), meso-acromion (middle), and the pre-acromion (tip). Failure of fusion of these
ossification centers may result in an os acromiale (Figure 1). This most commonly results
from failure of fusion between the meso-acromion and the meta-acromion and may be
associated with impingement and rotator cuff dysfunction.1 The Bigliani classification
can used to further classify the morphology of the acromion. Type I consists of a flat
acromion, type II consists of a curved acromion, and type III consists of a hooked
acromion2 (Figure 2). The association between acromial type, shoulder impingement,
and rotator cuff disease remains controversial.3,4 The Bigliani classification is further
limited by its poor interobserver reliability.5 The acromiohumeral interval is defined as
the space between the highest point of the humerus and the undersurface of the
acromion and generally ranges from 7 to 14 mm; however, a space less than 7 mm
increases suspicion of a massive rotator cuff tear.6 The acromion meets the clavicle to
form the diarthrodial acromioclavicular joint. Adjacent to the acromion, the scapular
spine traverses the length of the scapular body dividing the supraspinatus and
infraspinatus fossae. The scapular body articulates with the chest wall, generally
spanning the second through seventh ribs, and resides in a plane 30° anterior to the
body’s true coronal plane. The coracoid process projects anterolaterally from the scapula
and serves as an important point of reference during evaluation and surgical approaches
to the shoulder. The coracoid process is an important point of attachment for
ligamentous and muscular structures. These include the coracoacromial and
coracohumeral ligaments on its lateral side and the coracoclavicular ligaments attached
at its base. The coracobrachialis muscle and the short head of the biceps tendon
originate from the tip of the coracoid, and the pectoralis minor muscle inserts onto its
medial aspect. The suprascapular notch is located between the superior scapular body
and the medial base of the coracoid, whereas the spinoglenoid notch lies below the
lateral aspect of the scapular spine. The suprascapular nerve traverses the
suprascapular notch below the transverse scapular ligament as the suprascapular artery
courses above. The suprascapular nerve and artery then pass through the spinoglenoid

4/33

notch beneath the spinoglenoid ligament before terminating in the infraspinatus fossae.
These two anatomic sites may be sites of possible suprascapular nerve compression.
Figure 1: AP (A), outlet (B), and axillary lateral (C) radiographs of a right shoulder
demonstrate os acromiale. The os acromiale is most readily apparent on the axillary
lateral view (black arrow in panel C). (Reproduced from Kurtz CA, Humble BJ, Rodosky
MW, Sekiya JK: Symptomatic os acromiale. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2006 Jan;14[1]:12-19.)

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613

Figure 2: Illustrations (top) and corresponding supraspinatus outlet radiographs
(bottom) show the Bigliani classification of acromion morphology. (Reproduced with
permission from Pandey V, Jaap Willems W: Rotator cuff tear: A detailed update. Asia Pac
J Sports Med Arthrosc Rehabil Technol 2015;2[1]:1-14.)
Glenoid
The glenoid has a pear-shaped articular surface.
The subchondral bone of the glenoid is relatively flat and saucer-like. This shallow articular
concavity allows for a large degree of range of motion but requires additional augmentation by
cartilage and a circumferential labrum for added depth and stability.
The glenoid has a mean of 7° of retroversion in relation to the axis of the scapular body. The
glenoid has 5° of superior tilt.

Glenoid
The glenoid has an unusual articular pear-shape, which includes a broader inferior than
superior diameter with its longest dimension in its vertical axis. At the superior aspect of
the glenoid is the supraglenoid tubercle, which is the attachment site for the long head
of the biceps. The characteristic shallow and saucer-like articular surface is important for
permitting a large degree of glenohumeral motion; however, this is augmented by the
cartilage and labrum, which provide added depth and stability. The glenoid is retroverted
a mean of 7° to the axis of the scapula and has 5° of superior tilt.7
Superior Shoulder Suspensory Complex
The superior shoulder suspensory complex is an anatomic ring that consists of the glenoid,
coracoid process, coracoclavicular ligaments, distal clavicle, acromioclavicular joint, and
acromion.
The superior shoulder suspensory complex provides a stable connection between the scapula
and the axial skeleton.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
6/33

The superior strut comprises the middle clavicle; the inferior strut comprises the lateral
scapular border/spine of the scapula.

Superior Shoulder Suspensory Complex
The superior shoulder suspensory complex is an anatomic ring that consists of the
glenoid, coracoid process, distal clavicle, and acromion and their soft-tissue
interconnections via the coracoclavicular ligaments and the acromioclavicular joint
(Figure 3). The scapula is connected to the axial skeleton and suspended by the clavicle
and its attachments. A double disruption injury to this ring complex may cause instability
to the distal shoulder segment. This may result in subacromial impingement,
neurovascular compromise from a drooping shoulder, and adverse functional
imbalances, such as loss of the mechanical advantage of the rotator cuff, which may lead
to limitations in shoulder motion and weakness.8

Figure 3: Lateral view illustration shows the bone–soft-tissue ring of the superior
shoulder suspensory complex (dashed circle). (Reproduced from Goss TP: Scapular
fractures and dislocations: Diagnosis and treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1995;3[1]:22-
33.)
Proximal Humerus
The proximal humerus has three centers of ossification: the humeral head (4 to 6 months), the
greater tuberosity (1 to 3 years), and the lesser tuberosity (3 to 5 years). They fuse to the shaft
at age 17 to 20 years.
The humeral head has a mean of 25° of retroversion and a head-shaft angle of 135°.
The greater and lesser tuberosities serve as attachment sites for the rotator cuff tendons. The
subscapularis attaches to the lesser tuberosity, and the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and
teres minor attach to the greater tuberosity.
Historically, the anterior humeral circumflex artery was thought to provide the main blood
supply to the humeral head via its anterolateral ascending branch; however, currently, the
posterior humeral circumflex artery is known to provide most of the blood supply to the
humeral head.

Proximal Humerus
The proximal humerus has three centers of ossification, including the humeral head (4 to
6 months), greater tuberosity (1 to 3 years), and lesser tuberosity (3 to 5 years), which
fuse to the humeral shaft at age 17 to 20 years at a head-shaft angle of approximately
135°. The proximal humeral head has a mean of 25° of retroversion relative to the
transepicondylar axis of the elbow. The lesser tuberosity is the attachment site of the
subscapularis tendon and is in intimate proximity to the bicipital groove at its medial
border. The greater tuberosity is the attachment site for the remaining rotator cuff
tendons (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor). The posterior circumflex artery is
the primary blood supply to the articular segment of the humeral head (providing
approximately 64% of its perfusion), whereas the anterior humeral circumflex artery (via
the arcuate branch) contributes a smaller portion. The terminal portion of the artery
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
8/33

then makes an intraosseous course through the superolateral aspect of the
intertubercular groove into the greater tuberosity.9
Vascular Anatomy
Axillary Artery
The axillary artery is divided into three segments in relation to the pectoralis minor muscle.
First part (suprapectoral)
Medial to the pectoralis minor muscle
Has one branch: the superior thoracic artery
Second part (retropectoral)
Deep to the pectoralis minor muscle
Has two branches: the thoracoacromial trunk and the lateral thoracic artery
Third part (infrapectoral)
Lateral to the pectoralis minor muscle
Has three branches: the subscapular artery (the circumflex scapular branch runs through the
triangular space), the anterior humeral circumflex artery (the anterolateral ascending branch
contributes to blood supply to the humeral head), and the posterior humeral circumflex
artery (the dominant blood supply to the humeral head; accompanies the axillary nerve and
exits posteriorly through the quadrilateral space)

Axillary Artery
The axillary artery is a continuation of the subclavian artery and is officially identified
after traversing superficial to the first rib. The axillary artery subsequently passes deep
to the midshaft of the clavicle as it begins to branch and provide vascularization to the
shoulder. The axillary artery can be subdivided into three parts relative to its course
deep to the pectoralis minor (suprapectoral, retropectoral, infrapectoral). Each
subdivision of the axillary artery has sequentially increasing branches ranging from a
single branch in the suprapectoral region to three branches in the distal infrapectoral
region. For years, the primary blood supply to the proximal humerus was thought to be
the anterior humeral circumflex artery because it branches from the infrapectoral region
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
9/33

and courses along the inferior subscapularis tendon in combination with two veins. This
relationship is colloquially known as the three sisters and can be appreciated during the
deltopectoral approach. The posterior humeral circumflex artery is now known to be the
primary blood supply to the humeral head, also providing approximately 64% of the
vascularity to the proximal humerus and accompanying the axillary nerve as it exits
posteriorly through the quadrilateral space (medial: long head of the triceps; lateral:
humeral shaft; inferior: teres major; superior: teres minor). The circumflex scapular
branch passes through the triangular space (superior: teres minor; lateral: long head of
the triceps; inferior: teres major) as it provides vascularity to the dorsal scapula
musculature (Figure 4).
Figure 4: Illustration shows the vascularity of the anterior shoulder. (Adapted with
permission from Andary JL, Petersen SA: The vascular anatomy of the glenohumeral
capsule and ligaments: An anatomic study. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2002;84[12]:2258-2265.)
SEND FEEDBACK

Axillary Vein
Along its course, the axillary vein is positioned anteromedial to the axillary artery.
The venous return of the shoulder is highly variable and does not match arterial flow patterns.

Axillary Vein
The axillary vein serves as the venous return from the upper extremity and shoulder.
The axillary vein is positioned anteromedial to the axillary artery, and it courses along
the posterior border of the midshaft of the clavicle. The venous return and tributaries
throughout the shoulder are highly variable and do not follow the pattern of arterial
flow.10
Nerves
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
11/33

The brachial plexus is organized into roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and branches (Figure 5).
Figure 5: Illustration shows the brachial plexus and its terminal branches. (Adapted from
Thompson WO, Warren RF, Barnes RP, Hunt S: Shoulder injuries, in Schenck RC Jr, ed: Athletic
Training and Sports Medicine, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
1999, p 231.)

Nerves
The brachial plexus has a hierarchical structure consisting of roots, trunks, divisions,
cords, and branches originating from the C5-T1 nerve roots. This network of nerves is
responsible for innervating the motor and sensory functions to the chest, shoulder, arm,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
12/33

forearm, and hand. The plexus passes through the cervicoaxillary canal, over the first rib,
and into the axilla deep to the pectoralis minor muscle.
Axillary Nerve
The axillary nerve courses inferior to the glenohumeral joint, adjacent to the capsule, and is
closest to the glenoid labrum at the 6-o’clock position on the glenoid, at a mean of 12 mm.
The axillary nerve exits the axilla posteriorly, with the posterior humeral circumflex artery,
through the quadrilateral space (medial: long head of the triceps; lateral: humeral shaft;
superior: teres minor; inferior: teres major) before dividing into anterior and posterior
branches.
The posterior branch terminates into a muscular branch to the teres minor and a sensory
branch to the skin overlying the lateral deltoid (superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve). Loss
of sensation over the lateral deltoid may indicate palsy of the teres minor.
The muscular branch supplying the teres minor lies closest to the glenoid labrum and is most
susceptible to injury during arthroscopic capsular procedures.
The anterior branch courses along the undersurface and innervates the deltoid muscle.
Typically, the anterior branch to the deltoid is located 5 to 6 cm distal to the midlateral
acromial margin; however, it can be as close as 3 cm. This distance is positively correlated with
limb length; it is reduced by as much as 30% with abduction of the arm to 90°.

Axillary Nerve
The axillary nerve is a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (nerve roots:
C5-C6). It passes anterior to the subscapularis before exiting the axilla along the
subscapularis inferior border, subsequently passing medial to the surgical neck of the
humerus and 12 mm inferior to the glenoid. The axillary nerve then exits the
quadrilateral space and divides into three terminal branches (posterior, anterior, and
articular; Figure 6). The posterior terminal branch innervates the posterior aspect of the
deltoid and teres minor and provides innervation to the skin overlying the posterior and
lateral deltoid. The anterior terminal branch wraps around the surgical neck of the
humerus deep to the deltoid approximately 5 to 6 cm distal to the midlateral acromial
margin. This branch provides muscular innervation to the anterior deltoid andSEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
13/33

innervation to the skin overlying the anterior deltoid. Lastly, the articular branch of the
deltoid provides innervation to the glenohumeral joint. During the deltopectoral
approach, the tug test can be used to confirm the location of the axillary nerve by
placing a finger on the nerve at the inferior border of the subscapularis tendon and an
additional finger deep to the lateral deltoid at the location of the anterior terminal
branch. Gentle pressure will be translated across the course of the nerve and can be
appreciated by the examiner11 (Figure 7).
Figure 6: Illustration shows the muscles and nerves of the posterior aspect of the
shoulder. (Reproduced from Gramstad G: Anatomy of the shoulder, arm, and elbow, in
Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 715-726.)

Musculocutaneous Nerve
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
15/33

The main trunk penetrates the coracobrachialis muscle 3 to 8 cm distal to the tip of the
coracoid.
It innervates the biceps brachii and the brachialis.
It terminates as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve to the anterolateral forearm.

Musculocutaneous Nerve
The musculocutaneous nerve is a branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus (nerve
roots: C5-C7). It emerges from deep to the pectoralis minor before piercing the
coracobrachialis muscle 3 to 8 cm distal from the coracoid process. It then travels deep
to the biceps brachii but superficial to the brachialis before it emerges as the lateral
antebrachial cutaneous nerve and provides sensation to the anterolateral aspect of the
forearm. During its course, the musculocutaneous nerve provides motor innervation to
the coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, and brachialis.
Suprascapular Nerve
This nerve transverses through the suprascapular notch (under the superior transverse
scapular ligament), where it innervates the supraspinatus.
Posteriorly, it traverses the spinoglenoid notch to innervate the infraspinatus.
It is approximately 1.5 cm medial to the posterior rim of the glenoid and can be endangered in
this location with transglenoid fixation techniques.
Suprascapular nerve compression at the suprascapular notch causes denervation of the
supraspinatus and the infraspinatus. Nerve compression at the spinoglenoid notch leads to
selective denervation of the infraspinatus muscle.
Traction injury may result from repetitive overhead activity or secondary to a retracted rotator
cuff tear. Space-occupying lesions (eg, large perilabral cysts) may cause a direct compression
injury, typically at the spinoglenoid notch.

Suprascapular Nerve
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
16/33

The suprascapular nerve branches from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (nerve
roots: C5-C6). The nerve passes over the superior border of the scapula and through the
suprascapular notch medial to the base of the coracoid process. It then enters the
supraspinatus fossa before traversing along the lateral border of the scapular spine
through the spinoglenoid notch. It then terminates in the infraspinatus fossa of the
scapula. Two possible sites of compression are the suprascapular notch and the
spinoglenoid notch. The suprascapular nerve innervates the supraspinatus and
infraspinatus muscles.
Long Thoracic Nerve
Injury (from axillary dissection or aggressive retraction of the middle scalene muscle) results in
serratus anterior palsy and medial winging of the scapula (superior elevation of the scapula
with medial translation and medial rotation of the inferior pole of the scapula).

Long Thoracic Nerve
The long thoracic nerve arises from the anterior rami of the C5 through C7 nerve roots
to innervate the serratus anterior muscle. It is located on the superficial surface of the
serratus anterior muscle, making it susceptible to injury, which may result in
characteristic medial winging of the scapula.
Spinal Accessory Nerve (Cranial Nerve XI)
Injury from cervical lymph node biopsy or radical neck dissection results in trapezius palsy and
lateral winging of the scapula (depression of the scapula with lateral translation and lateral
rotation of the inferior pole of the scapula).

Spinal Accessory Nerve (Cranial Nerve XI)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
17/33

The spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) innervates the trapezius, which attaches to
the acromion, scapular spine, and clavicle. Subsequent injury to the spinal accessory
nerve may result in lateral winging of the scapula.
Joints and Ligaments
Sternoclavicular Joint
The sternoclavicular joint is the only true diarthrodial articulation between the upper
appendicular and axial skeletons.
The posterior sternoclavicular joint capsule and ligaments are the primary stabilizers to
anterior and posterior translation of the medial clavicle.

Sternoclavicular Joint
The sternoclavicular joint connects the shoulder to the axial skeleton via the clavicle. A
fibrocartilaginous disk is interposed between the clavicle and sternum. The
sternoclavicular joint is stabilized primarily by its posterior capsular ligaments, which
prevent anterior, posterior, and inferior displacement. The anterior capsular ligaments
restrict superior displacement of the medial clavicle.12
Acromioclavicular Joint
The acromioclavicular joint is a small diarthrodial joint with an interposed fibrocartilaginous
disk.
The superior and posterior acromioclavicular ligaments are the primary stabilizers to anterior
and posterior (horizontal) translation of the clavicle.
The coracoclavicular ligaments (conoid: medial; trapezoid: lateral) are the primary stabilizers to
superior (vertical) translation of the distal clavicle.

Acromioclavicular Joint
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:30 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Anatomy and Function
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000613
18/33

Similar to the sternoclavicular joint, the acromioclavicular joint is a diarthrodial joint with
an interposed fibrocartilaginous disk. The superior and posterior ligaments confer the
greatest degree of horizontal stability to the joint; however, the adjacent coracoclavicular
ligaments provide the greatest resistance to superior translation of the clavicle that is
classically observed in patients with acromioclavicular joint separations and distal
clavicle fractures.
Glenohumeral Joint
Dynamic stabilizers—The rotator cuff stabilizes the joint via joint compression. Positioning of
the scapulothoracic joint also contributes to dynamic stability.
Static stabilizers include articular congruity, the glenoid labrum, concavity-compression,
negative intra-articular pressure, and the glenohumeral capsule and ligaments. The glenoid
labrum provides concavity and as much as 50% of marginal glenoid socket depth.
The rotator interval is defined medially by the base of the coracoid, superiorly by the
supraspinatus tendon, and inferiorly by the subscapularis tendon.
The rotator interval contains the coracohumeral ligament, the superior glenohumeral ligament
(SGHL), and the intra-articular portion of the long head of the biceps tendon. Laxity of the
rotator interval results in inferior laxity (the sulcus sign), and contracture of the interval is
observed in patients with adhesive capsulitis.
The coracohumeral ligament restricts external rotation in adduction, and it is a static restraint
to inferior and posterior translation in adduction and external rotation.
The SGHL is a primary static restraint against anterior translation with the arm at the side.
With the coracohumeral ligament, the SGHL forms a pulley that provides restraint against
medial subluxation of the long head of the biceps tendon.
The middle glenohumeral ligament (MGHL) is a primary static restraint against anterior
translation with the arm in external rotation and 45° of abduction.
The anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament is a primary static restraint against
anteroinferior dislocation of the glenohumeral joint in 90° of abduction and external rotation
(position of apprehension).
The posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament is a primary static restraint against
posteroinferior translation in internal rotation and adduction.


Glenohumeral Joint
Compared with other joints in the body, the glenohumeral joint has the greatest range of
mobility. This is largely attributed to its lack of bony constraint. To achieve joint stability,
a complex balance of dynamic and static stabilizers is present. The dynamic stability of
the glenohumeral joint is enforced by the compressive forces of the rotator cuff
balancing the round humeral head on the saucer-like glenoid. The rotator cuff resists the
superior pull of the deltoid while keeping the humerus centered on the glenoid fulcrum.
This is essential for the deltoid to power motion of the humerus because loss of the
stabilizing forces of the rotator cuff (such as in patients with a massive rotator cuff tear)
may lead to pseudoparalysis of the shoulder. The static stabilizers provide stability at the
extremes of motion, whereas the dynamic stabilizers confer glenohumeral stability
throughout functional range of motion. The static stabilizers include the articular
congruity, which is further deepened by the glenoid labrum, concavity-compression
(articulation permitting rotation but preventing translational movement), negative intra-
articular pressure, and the glenohumeral capsule and ligaments. The glenoid fossa is
most susceptible to anterior and posterior shear force instability, partly because the
glenoid has less depth in the anteroposterior dimension than in the superoinferior
dimension.13 The superior, middle, and inferior glenohumeral ligaments play important
roles in resisting anterior instability at gradually increasing degrees of shoulder
abduction, respectively. The posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament also
plays a role in resisting posterior stability (Figure 8).
The long head of the biceps tendon is secured in the bicipital groove by the transverse
humeral ligament, which is a critical stabilizer that bridges the lesser and greater
tuberosities of the humerus. This fibrous band ensures the tendon remains in place
during shoulder movement, preventing it from subluxating or dislocating. The integrity
of the transverse humeral ligament, along with the coracohumeral ligament and the
SGHL, is essential to the pulley system that anchors the biceps tendon, contributing to
the complex biomechanics of the shoulder joint. In addition, the transverse humeral
ligament spans the bicipital groove and helps secure the long head of the biceps tendon
in place, working in combination with the SGHL and the coracohumeral ligament as part
of the biceps pulley system.

The scapulothoracic joint is an area of articulation lubricated by bursae between the scapula
and thorax.
The scapula’s primary motion is elevation and depression; however, protraction and retraction
also are important secondary motions for clearance of the humeral head with overhead
activities.
With every 2° to 3° of shoulder abduction at the glenohumeral joint, 1° of motion occurs at the
scapulothoracic joint.

Scapulothoracic Joint
The scapulothoracic joint works in concert with the glenohumeral joint to facilitate arm
range of motion. This coordinated movement is termed scapulohumeral rhythm. For
every 2° to 3° of shoulder abduction at the glenohumeral joint, 1° of motion occurs at
the scapulothoracic joint14 (Figure 9). With full shoulder abduction of 180°, 120° of
shoulder motion is contributed from the glenohumeral joint, with the remaining 60°
originating from the scapulothoracic joint. The scapula rotates upward with the
assistance of the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. Secondary motion of the
scapulothoracic joint includes protraction and retraction, which facilitates clearance of
the humeral head with overhead activities.

Deltopectoral Approach
This is the main approach to the shoulder.
It uses the internervous plane between the deltoid (axillary nerve) and the pectoralis major
(medial and lateral pectoral nerves) muscles.
The cephalic vein usually is present in the interval.
The clavipectoral fascia overlies the conjoined tendon (coracobrachialis and short head of the
biceps) and the subscapularis.
The musculocutaneous nerve is at risk for retraction injury medially.
The axillary nerve (posterior cord of the brachial plexus) can be palpated on the anteroinferior
surface of the subscapularis, medial to the coracoid.
The anterior circumflex humeral artery travels along the inferior subscapularis between the
upper two-thirds and the inferior one-third (muscular portion).

Deltopectoral Approach
The deltopectoral approach is the most common approach used for open shoulder
surgery. It follows the internervous plane between the deltoid (axillary nerve) and the
pectoralis major (medial and lateral pectoral nerves). Advantages of this approach are its
extensile nature and its limited scarring because of the use of anatomic planes; however,
it is limited in its ability to manage posterior shoulder pathology and the need for
takedown and subsequent repair of the subscapularis tendon (Video 1).

Lateral Deltoid Split Approach
The lateral approach is commonly used for repair of the rotator cuff and greater tuberosity
fractures.
A mini-open approach to the shoulder uses a deltoid split. The axillary nerve branch to the
anterior deltoid is at risk of injury with this approach.
Alternatively, the deltoid is detached from the anterolateral acromion for wider exposure.

Lateral Deltoid Split Approach
The deltoid split approach involves the use of a nonanatomic interval between the
anterior and middle heads of the deltoid. Advantages of this approach are direct
exposure to the tuberosities and an in-line approach to the glenoid during arthroplasty;
however, this approach is limited because it is nonextensile and places the axillary nerve
at increased risk15 (Figure 10).

The posterior approach is commonly used for posterior capsular shift procedures and repair
of glenoid fractures. Latissimus dorsi release (for transfer) also can be performed with this
approach. The radial nerve lies anterior to the latissimus dorsi insertion on the humerus and is
at risk of injury with tendon release.
Identification of the quadrilateral space protects the axillary nerve and the posterior
circumflex humeral artery.
This approach involves the use of the internervous plane between the teres minor (axillary
nerve) inferiorly and the infraspinatus (suprascapular nerve) superiorly.

Posterior Approach
The posterior approach involves the use of the internervous plane between the teres
minor (axillary nerve) and the infraspinatus (suprascapular nerve). The advantages of
this approach are excellent exposure to posterior-based structures and access to the
scapular neck and body (Video 2).

Arthroscopic Anatomy of the Shoulder
The long head of the biceps brachii exits the joint in the lateral aspect of the rotator interval
and is stabilized against medial subluxation by the subscapularis (deep fibers) and a pulley
composed of the coracohumeral ligament and the SGHL.
The superior biceps–labral anchor complex is anchored to the supraglenoid tubercle. A mobile
and/or meniscoid superior glenoid labrum associated with an extension of articular cartilage
over the superior glenoid rim may be a normal variant and must be differentiated from a
traumatic disruption of the superior labrum (superior labral anterior to posterior tear) from
bone.
The region of the anterosuperior labrum and MGHL origin has wide anatomic variability.
The most common anatomy is an attached labrum with a broad MGHL.
A sublabral foramen often is associated with a cordlike MGHL.
A cordlike MGHL with an absent anterosuperior labrum is a rare variant known as the Buford
complex.
The glenoid chondrolabral junction does not define the margin of the osseous glenoid in its
inferior half. The glenoid labrum overlies the osseous glenoid face from 2 to 7 mm in this
region.
A central bare spot on the glenoid and a bare area on the posterior humeral head, adjacent to
the infraspinatus insertion, normally are devoid of cartilage and are not representative of
trauma or arthritis.

Arthroscopic Anatomy of the Shoulder
Arthroscopic shoulder surgery is a minimally invasive technique that affords a large
degree of visualization and access to multiple glenohumeral and subacromial structures.
The standard portals are placed in the posterior, anterior, and lateral aspects of the
shoulder. The long head of the biceps is an important intra-articular structure that can
be used as an anatomic reference for navigating the glenohumeral joint and aids in
identifying adjacent structures such as the labrum and MGHL; however, wide anatomic
variation in the labrum and MGHL exists (Figure 11 ; Video 3 ) .
